newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan says opens Uganda front in rebel conflict.
newsitem.headline: Sudan says opens Uganda front in rebel conflict.

text.p: Sudan said on Sunday it had attacked a rebel base near the southern border with Uganda, opening another front in the war against rebels trying to overthrow the Islamist government.
Rebels and the government have previously reported clashes in the east, near the Ethiopian and Eritrean borders.

State television quoted Information Minister Brigadier Al-Tayeb Ibrahim Mohamed Khair as saying the armed forces had killed several rebels and routed others in fighting which took place at Lokia, an area near the southern town of Torit about 75 km (47 miles) from the Uganda border.

"Several rebels were killed and wounded and a big number of heavy and light guns was seized," he said without giving any exact figures. "The rebels were chased away and the armed forces sustained a few wounded."
It was the first report of clashes so far south. There have been no independent accounts of the fighting in Sudan and it is difficult to assess the veracity of reports issued by the two sides.

The Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), a mainly southern group which has been fighting the army in southern Sudan since 1983, is now working together with the northern opposition to Sudan's Islamist government.

SPLA leader John Garang says rebel strategy is to overthrow the government through war in the east and south and political action in Khartoum, where they hope for the kind of popular uprising which ended previous periods of military rule.
A Sudanese official was quoted on Sunday as saying government troops had killed opposition fighters in the east.
The official Sudan News Agency quoted Ali Maget, the head of Roseires town which is the site of a strategic dam, as saying the clash took place just south of the town in Um Darfa.

"The armed forces responded decisively to an attack launched by the Tigrean (Ethiopian) forces and the attack (on the Ethiopians) killed a big number of the attackers, forcing the rest to flee into Ethiopia," Maget said.
The Sudanese government of President Omar Hassan al-Bashir says hostile neighbours Eritrea and Ethiopia are fighting with rebels, but both states deny any part in the fighting.

The state radio Omdurman said the Sudanese government has formed a body to oversee general mobilisation in the country. It did not say when President al-Bashir issued the decree forming the so-called High Authority for Mobilisation.

The new body is charged with planning mobilisation activities, maintaining national unity and collecting money to support the armed forces, the radio said. It will also gather information on the war in local and international media.
The radio said Vice President Al-Zubeir Mohamed Saleh would head the 45-member body which also includes ministers of defence, internal affairs, health, federal rule and information.
In Cairo, the National Democratic Alliance, which groups southern and northern rebels, charged Iran with helping the state army with chemical weapons and troops.

"In the past few days, Iran has supplied Sudan with large amounts of heavy and light weapons, goods and chemical weapons to use against the rebels," NDA Secretary-General Mubarak Mahdi said in a faxed statement.
He said that Iran had also sent 60 Russian-made tanks, six aircraft, several weapons experts and pilots to take part in the fighting in the south and east.
Iran has good ties with the Khartoum government and mediated a peace deal between Uganda and Sudan late last year.

The rebels say their aim is to take the key southeastern town of Damazin, which the government is using as the pivot of its counterattack. A Sudanese government-owned daily said the state had sent 3,000 more volunteer troops to the southeast.
Damazin is near the strategic Roseires Dam which provides Khartoum with most of its electricity and the rebels say they are only a few kilometres away, a claim which Sudan denies.
